title: Photography and Hyper-Realism
answer: Synthetic portraiture, lighting rigs, upscaling, product mockups and virtual location scouting.

children.name: Synthetic Portraiture
children.blurb: Synthetic portraiture is the creation of photographic or hyper-realistic images of human faces and figures that do not depict a real person.

sections.body: Photography and hyper-realism in AI covers the use of machine learning to produce or alter images that look like photographs. Current work includes generating faces for synthetic portraiture, changing the direction and color of light in existing photos, enlarging low resolution images while reducing grain, placing products into lifestyle scenes, and creating previews of possible filming locations. These systems learn from large sets of photographs and then apply that learning to new pixels. The output is often indistinguishable from a real photo at a glance, but it is still a reconstruction rather than a capture of light.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The site currently tracks no live image generation models, so this section describes techniques and workflows rather than specific tools. Synthetic faces are now common in advertising and stock imagery, but fine details like teeth, ears, and hair strands can still break down under close inspection. Relighting works well for simple scenes but struggles with complex materials like translucent skin or brushed metal. Upscaling can recover plausible texture, yet it may invent details that were never in the original. Product mockups are reliable for simple shapes and fabrics, but reflective or deformable objects often look wrong. Virtual location scouting can produce useful concept images, but it cannot verify physical access, lighting conditions, or legal permissions.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for how fake but realistic people are made would start with Synthetic Portraiture, which covers face generation and identity control. Lighting Rigs and Relighting then explains how to change the mood of an image after it was taken, which is useful for both portraits and products. Upscaling and Noise Reduction addresses the common problem of low resolution or grainy source material, and it pairs naturally with the other pages because most generated or edited images need cleanup. Product and Fashion Mockups shows how the same techniques are applied to commercial photography, where a garment or object is placed into a scene without a physical shoot. Virtual Location Scouting moves from objects and people to whole environments, using similar image synthesis to preview places before committing to travel or set construction.
